mlworkflow.q: What is the test set for?
options: Choosing hyperparameters such as tree depth
Training the model's weights
Measuring final performance once, after all choices are made
Filling in missing values
mlworkflow.why: The test set is opened once at the end. Using it to tune settings turns it into another validation set and makes the final number optimistic.

mlworkflow.q: A model scores 0.99 on training data and 0.72 on validation data. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Overfitting: it memorised noise in the training rows
Underfitting: the model is too simple
The validation set is too large
The learning rate is too small
mlworkflow.why: A big gap with a high training score is the classic sign of overfitting. Underfitting shows low scores on both.

mlworkflow.q: A customer says their fraud model has 98 percent accuracy. Fraud is 2 percent of transactions. What do you ask for first?
options: A bigger training set
The baseline and recall on fraud cases
A switch to a neural network
The model's training time
mlworkflow.why: Always predicting 'not fraud' also scores 98 percent. Compare with that baseline and check how much fraud is actually caught.

mlworkflow.q: You are predicting next month's sales from three years of monthly data. How should you split?
options: Random 80/20 split with shuffle
Stratify by product category
Use the whole dataset for training and test
Train on earlier months, validate and test on later months
mlworkflow.why: The model will predict the future, so the split must too. A random split lets it learn from months after the ones it is scored on.

mlworkflow.q: Spot the mistake: 'We scaled all rows with StandardScaler, then ran 5-fold cross-validation on the scaled data.'
options: StandardScaler should be MinMaxScaler
5 folds is too few
The scaler learned from validation rows; it should sit inside a Pipeline
Cross-validation should never be used with scaling
mlworkflow.why: Fitting any transformer before splitting leaks information from validation rows into training. Inside a Pipeline it is refitted on each training fold.

featureeng.q: What does one-hot encoding do to a column with values basic, pro and team?
options: Replaces them with 1, 2 and 3
Makes three 0/1 columns, one per value
Replaces each value with its churn rate
Drops the column because models cannot use text
featureeng.why: One-hot makes one indicator column per category. Numbering them 1, 2, 3 would invent an order that does not exist.

featureeng.q: Why add a was_missing flag when you impute a column?
options: Because the fact a value was missing can itself predict the outcome
Because scikit-learn requires it
To make the model train faster
To remove outliers
featureeng.why: Missing values are often not random, for example applicants refusing to give income. The flag lets the model use that signal.

featureeng.q: A store_id column has 3,000 distinct values. Which encoding is the most sensible first try?
options: One-hot encoding with 3,000 columns
Numbering stores 1 to 3,000
Smoothed, cross-fitted target encoding
Dropping the column without testing it
featureeng.why: Target encoding keeps one column and captures each store's typical outcome. Smoothing and cross fitting stop small stores and leakage from fooling it.

featureeng.q: Your live scoring job crashes when a new plan type appears. What is the fix?
options: Retrain the model every hour
Delete rows with new plans
Switch to a tree model
Use OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") inside the saved Pipeline
featureeng.why: handle_unknown="ignore" encodes an unseen category as all zeros instead of raising an error, and the Pipeline applies it the same way in training and live.

featureeng.q: Spot the trap: a churn feature is 'days since last login', computed on the day the data was exported.
options: It should be in weeks, not days
It includes time after the prediction moment, so it leaks the outcome
It needs one-hot encoding
It should be scaled with MinMaxScaler
featureeng.why: Customers who already left have large values only because they left. Compute durations as of each prediction date.

linreg.q: In y = w * x + b, what does w mean?
options: The prediction when x is zero
The average of all y values
The size of the error
How much y changes when x rises by one unit
linreg.why: w is the slope, the change in prediction per unit of x. b is the intercept, the prediction at x = 0.

options: The sum of squared residuals
The largest single error
The number of wrong predictions
The sum of the weights
linreg.why: Least squares picks weights that make the total of squared gaps between actual and predicted values as small as possible.

linreg.q: Your gradient descent loss jumps up and down and then grows each step. What do you try first?
options: Add more features
Increase the learning rate
Lower the learning rate and check features are scaled
Remove the intercept
linreg.why: Steps that are too big overshoot the bottom of the loss bowl. A smaller learning rate and scaled features make descent stable.

linreg.q: A courier asks how accurate your delivery time model is. Which number do you lead with?
options: The training R squared
MAE in minutes on validation data
The number of coefficients
The learning rate
linreg.why: MAE is in the customer's units ('typically 11 minutes off') and measured on unseen data. Training R squared can flatter the model.

linreg.q: Spot the mistake: 'Removing one broken-down van trip changed our slope from 12.8 to 4.0 minutes per km, but it is only one row, so it cannot matter.'
options: One extreme outlier can drag least squares a lot because errors are squared
The slope should not change at all
The model needs lasso instead
The intercept is wrong, not the slope
linreg.why: Squaring makes a huge error dominate the loss. Check residuals, investigate outliers, or use a robust model such as HuberRegressor.

logreg.q: What does the sigmoid function do in logistic regression?
options: Picks the most important feature
Squashes any score into a probability between 0 and 1
Removes missing values
Chooses the threshold
logreg.why: The sigmoid maps the weighted sum z to 1 / (1 + e^-z), which is always between 0 and 1. z = 0 gives exactly 0.5.

logreg.q: The model gives 0.01 probability to a case that really was positive. What happens to log loss?
options: Nothing, it only counts wrong classes
It drops, because the model was confident
It rises sharply, because the model was confidently wrong
It becomes exactly 0.5
logreg.why: Log loss for that row is -log(0.01), about 4.6. Confident mistakes are punished far more than hesitant ones.

logreg.q: A fraud team can review 70 cases a day. The model flags 45 at threshold 0.5. What do you suggest?
options: Lower the threshold until about 70 cases are flagged
Keep 0.5, because it is the standard
Raise the threshold to improve precision
Retrain with more features before any change
logreg.why: The threshold is a business choice. Lowering it uses the team's capacity to catch more fraud, at some cost in precision.

logreg.q: A coefficient for 'support tickets' is 0.7. How do you explain it to a customer?
options: Each ticket adds 0.7 percent churn probability
Each ticket causes churn 70 percent of the time
Tickets are 0.7 times as important as other features
Each extra ticket roughly doubles the odds of churn, other things equal
logreg.why: exp(0.7) is about 2.0, the odds ratio. It is an association in this data, not proof that tickets cause churn.

logreg.q: Spot the trap: churn is 2 percent, the model has 98 percent accuracy, so the team ships it at threshold 0.5.
options: 98 percent is too low for production
It may flag no churners at all; check recall and choose a lower threshold or class weights
Logistic regression cannot do binary problems
The threshold should be 0.98 to match accuracy
logreg.why: With rare positives, always saying no scores 98 percent. Check recall and precision, and use threshold tuning or class_weight="balanced".
